name: Simply Piano
tagline: A piano learning app that listens to you play through the mic or a MIDI cable and grades each note against a scrolling score.

pricing.notes: AI-drafted from a site submission; price unverified.

verdictSummary: The mechanic is not the hard part: Web MIDI plus a notation renderer plus a timing judge is a weekend, and an agent will get you a working note-reading drill in one sitting. What you cannot one-shot is the thing people actually pay for, which is a few hundred graded song arrangements of music you recognize, licensed, fingered, and sequenced into a curriculum that does not dump a beginner into a Chopin prelude. The audio side is also harder than it looks: single-note pitch detection from a laptop mic is a textbook autocorrelation exercise, but hearing a sustained acoustic chord over room noise and a sustain pedal and deciding which of four notes you fluffed is a tuned-model problem, not an afternoon. A DIY build is genuinely useful if you own a MIDI keyboard and only want sight-reading practice on public domain scores. It is not a replacement for the lesson path.
coreLoopDIY: Renders a score, listens to your MIDI keyboard, and scores each note for pitch and timing as a playhead scrolls.
requirements: A MIDI keyboard or digital piano with USB, Chrome or Edge for Web MIDI
Node 20+ and a browser, everything runs locally
MusicXML or MIDI files you are legally allowed to use, public domain scores from IMSLP or the Mutopia Project
Optional: a mic and tolerance for flaky monophonic pitch detection if you have no MIDI cable
whatYouLose: The licensed catalog of pop songs arranged at five difficulty levels, which is most of the reason beginners stick with it
A curriculum that orders skills sensibly instead of handing you a folder of files
Reliable acoustic listening, chord detection through a phone mic in a real room is the actual engineering
iOS and Android apps, streaks, and the nagging that makes you practice on a Tuesday
Hand position and fingering guidance, your build only knows whether the right pitch arrived on time
moatNotes: Song licensing is the quiet wall. Any clone that wants recognizable music either pays publishers or stays in the 1800s.
whyPeopleStillPay: Because the product is not a note detector, it is a path. Someone who has never played wants to be playing something they recognize within a week, with the difficulty creeping up behind their back, and that requires a licensed catalog plus arrangers plus pedagogy, none of which falls out of a code generator. The mic listening also carries real weight for the large group of users who own an acoustic upright and no MIDI cable, and that path is a tuned audio model, not an npm package. A self-hosted sight-reading trainer scratches a different, narrower itch.
notes: The note judge is a weekend build; the song library is not. The moat is licensed arrangements, a curriculum ordering them, and an audio model that can hear a chord on a real piano in a real room.
prompt:
Build a local piano sight-reading trainer called Keys. Single page web app, no backend, no accounts, no telemetry, no cloud.
Stack: Vite + TypeScript + vanilla DOM. VexFlow for notation rendering. Web MIDI API for input. Tone.js for metronome and playback. No framework, no router, no state library.
Runs with: npm install, npm run dev, open localhost in Chrome.
In scope:
1. Load exercises from /public/scores as MIDI files, parsed with @tonejs/midi. Ship three hand-written exercises as MIDI: C major scale, a simple five-finger pattern, and one short public domain piece (Bach, Notebook for Anna Magdalena, Minuet in G).
2. Render the active exercise as notation with VexFlow, treble and bass staves, with a playhead that advances in time with the metronome.
3. Connect to a MIDI keyboard via Web MIDI. Show a device picker and a live list of held notes so the user can confirm the cable works before starting.
4. Judging: for each expected note, open a timing window of +/- 150ms around its onset. Mark hit, wrong pitch, early, late, or missed. Color the notehead green, red, or amber as it is judged.
5. Scoring: percent correct, average timing offset in ms, and a per-exercise best score stored in localStorage.
6. Tempo control from 40 to 160 BPM, count-in of one bar, loop-the-section mode where the user drags to select bars and practices only those.
7. A practice log view: date, exercise, tempo, score, read from localStorage, rendered as a plain table.
Out of scope, do not build: microphone pitch detection, chord detection from audio, user accounts, any server, any copyrighted song, fingering hints, video lessons, mobile apps.
Add a MIC_INPUT_TODO.md explaining honestly that monophonic mic detection via autocorrelation is a later add-on and polyphonic acoustic detection is out of reach for this build.
No secrets are needed, so no .env. If you later add any API, read keys from .env and commit .env.example only.
Keep all logic in src/ with files under 300 lines: midi-input.ts, judge.ts, score-render.ts, transport.ts, storage.ts, main.ts.
Write a README with setup, which browsers support Web MIDI, and where to drop additional public domain MIDI files.
